body:
What is a ledger?

A ledger is a record of transactions or events. Traditionally, a ledger might record payments, the transfer of goods or changes in ownership. A digital ledger performs the same basic function electronically.

Consider 3 organisations involved in transporting agricultural produce: a farmers' cooperative, a transport company and a warehouse. Each organisation may maintain its own records. If those records disagree, the organisations must determine which entry is correct. A shared digital ledger can help them maintain a consistent history of accepted transactions.

Meaning of distributed ledger technology

Distributed ledger technology (DLT) is a method of recording and maintaining data at multiple locations within a network, according to agreed rules. Participating computers, called nodes, can hold and update copies of the shared record.

The important feature is not merely that data exists on several computers. Ordinary databases can also have backup copies. In a distributed ledger, the participating organisations use defined procedures to validate and agree on additions to the shared record.

Different nodes may perform different functions. Some maintain full copies, some validate transactions and others have more limited access. Therefore, a distributed ledger does not require every participant to store every record.

What makes a blockchain different?

A blockchain is a type of distributed ledger in which accepted records are organised into a sequence of blocks. Each new block contains a cryptographic link to an earlier block, usually the immediately preceding one. This linking makes unauthorised changes to earlier records easier to detect.

Blockchain is therefore a particular method of organising and protecting a ledger. Other distributed ledgers may use different arrangements for recording data.

Every blockchain is a form of distributed ledger, but not every distributed ledger is a blockchain. The broader term is DLT.

How a shared ledger differs from a conventional database

In a conventional centralised database, an organisation normally controls the authoritative record. It can grant access to employees or other organisations and may maintain several backup servers. This arrangement is often efficient when all users trust the central organisation.

In a distributed ledger, several participating entities can maintain a shared history under agreed validation rules. This can be useful when more than one organisation needs to contribute records and no single organisation should have unrestricted control over the history.

A blockchain is not automatically better than a conventional database. It introduces additional coordination, storage and governance requirements. Where one trusted organisation is responsible for the data, an ordinary database may be simpler and more suitable.

Blockchain is not the same as cryptocurrency

Cryptocurrency is a digital asset that may use blockchain technology to record transfers. Bitcoin is a well-known example. Blockchain itself is a record-keeping technology and can also support certificates, supply-chain records and other applications that do not involve cryptocurrency.

Similarly, digitising a document, creating an online portal or maintaining electronic land records does not, by itself, make a system blockchain-based.

Prelims focus

  • A ledger records transactions or events.
  • DLT maintains shared records at multiple network locations under agreed rules.
  • Blockchain links blocks of accepted records cryptographically.
  • DLT is the broader category; blockchain is one type of DLT.
  • Blockchain can be used without cryptocurrency.
  • Trap: Multiple database backups do not, by themselves, establish that a system uses blockchain.

[National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Blockchain, overview, consulted 5 November 2026; UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Introduction and Distributed Ledger Technology sections, consulted 5 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Chapter 7, Tertiary and Quaternary Activities, pp. 58–59, for the foundations of communication and information services.]

title: Blockchain and Distributed Ledgers: Meaning and Basic Principles

body:
From a transaction to an accepted record

A blockchain records transactions or other events accepted under the rules of its network. A transaction may represent a transfer of a digital asset, the issue of a certificate or an update to a shared register.

The basic process involves the following activities:

  1. Submission: A participant submits a proposed transaction or record.
  2. Validation: The network checks the proposal against applicable rules, such as whether the participant is authorised and whether the record is properly formed.
  3. Agreement: The network follows its consensus procedure to determine which valid records are accepted and in what order.
  4. Recording: Accepted records are included in the ledger. In a blockchain, records are organised into cryptographically linked blocks.
  5. Updating: Participating nodes update their ledger copies according to the network rules.

The exact order of block proposal, validation and acceptance varies between blockchain systems. What matters is that the recorded history follows the system's agreed rules.

Blocks and cryptographic hashes

A block contains accepted transaction information and information needed to connect it to the existing blockchain. A cryptographic hash is a fixed-length digital value calculated from specified data. It works like a digital fingerprint: changing the underlying data will ordinarily produce a different hash.

In a typical blockchain, a block contains a cryptographic reference to the previous block. If someone changes an earlier block, the hash associated with that block changes. The later block's stored reference would then disagree with the altered data. This inconsistency helps reveal tampering.

Cryptographic links work together with distributed copies and consensus rules. An attacker cannot normally make an accepted historical change merely by editing one local copy. Other participants can detect that the altered copy does not agree with the recognised ledger history.

Meaning of immutability

Immutability is the property that makes accepted historical records difficult to change without detection and, under the network's security assumptions, difficult to replace.

Blockchain records are commonly described as immutable, but this does not mean that alteration is mathematically impossible under every circumstance. The strength of immutability depends on the network's design, participating validators, security controls and governance.

An important practical consequence is that an incorrect record is generally corrected through a later authorised entry, rather than silently replacing the original historical entry. The history can then show both the original record and the correction.

Correcting a certificate record

Suppose an institution records that a certificate has been issued. Later, it discovers a mistake in the certificate. Instead of secretly changing the historical issue record, the system can add an authorised correction or revocation entry. A verifier should check the current status as well as the original issue information.

Hashing, digital signatures and truthfulness

These concepts perform different functions:

  • Hash: Helps detect whether specified data has changed.
  • Digital signature: Provides evidence that a transaction was signed using a particular private key and that the signed information has not been altered. Linking the key to a real person's identity requires appropriate identity checks.
  • Consensus: Determines the records and order that the network accepts under its rules.

None of these mechanisms guarantees that the original statement was true. If an authorised official enters an incorrect date, the blockchain may preserve a reliable record of that incorrect entry. Accurate data collection and responsible verification remain necessary.

Nor does hashing mean that information is encrypted or hidden. Hashing checks integrity; encryption protects the confidentiality of readable information. A blockchain does not automatically keep all recorded information private.

Prelims focus

  • Blocks in a blockchain are connected using cryptographic references.
  • A hash helps reveal changes to the data from which it was calculated.
  • Immutability means tamper resistance, not an unconditional impossibility of alteration.
  • Errors can be addressed through later correction or revocation entries.
  • A digital signature and a hash perform different functions.
  • Trap: An unchanged blockchain entry is not necessarily a factually correct entry.

[NIST, Blockchain, explanation of blocks, cryptographic links, tamper evidence and network copies, consulted 5 November 2026; NIST, Blockchain Technology Overview, NISTIR 8202, October 2018, overview of blockchain records and cryptographic mechanisms; UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Distributed Ledger Technology section, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Changing an earlier block disrupts the cryptographic links to later blocks.

title: How Blockchain Records Are Linked and Why They Resist Tampering

body:
Why consensus is necessary

A distributed ledger may have several computers receiving transactions at different times. Two proposed records may conflict. For example, in a digital payment system, a participant might try to spend the same available funds twice. The network needs a method to decide which valid transactions become part of its accepted history.

Consensus is the process by which a distributed network reaches agreement on the accepted state or history of its ledger according to established rules.

Consensus keeps participating nodes from maintaining permanently conflicting versions of the authoritative history. It concerns the acceptance and ordering of transactions, not agreement about every statement made by a person.

Consensus also does not necessarily mean that every participant votes or that all participants agree unanimously. Different networks use different rules, eligible validators and thresholds.

What happens during consensus?

At a basic level, the network must distinguish valid proposals from invalid ones, handle competing proposals and determine which accepted records should be added. Participating nodes then update their records according to that decision.

Consider a shared certificate register. If an unauthorised person submits a certificate-issue record, the register should reject it under the applicable permission rules. If an authorised institution submits a properly formed entry, eligible validators can consider it for acceptance. The system's consensus rules determine how the accepted entry becomes part of the common history.

Major consensus approaches

ApproachBasic principleTypical setting or example
Proof of Work (PoW)Participants called miners perform computational work to compete in adding blocks.Bitcoin
Proof of Stake (PoS)Validators participate by committing stake under network rules; dishonest behaviour may lead to penalties.Ethereum since September 2022
Permissioned validationIdentified, authorised participants validate and agree on records under rules set by the network.Government or business networks with approved members

Proof of Work uses substantial computing effort. It can provide security in an open network but may consume considerable electricity. The scale of energy use depends on the network and its operating conditions.

Proof of Stake relies on economic stake and protocol-defined rewards or penalties rather than PoW-style competition in computational work. Ethereum changed from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake in September 2022. Bitcoin continues to use Proof of Work.

In a permissioned network, the authorised validators may be known organisations, such as government departments or regulated institutions. Such networks can use different consensus procedures; there is no single consensus method required for every permissioned blockchain.

Consensus is not the same as validation or immutability

Validation checks whether a proposed record obeys the rules. Consensus establishes which valid records become the accepted network history. Immutability makes that accepted history difficult to alter afterward. The concepts work together but are not interchangeable.

Consensus cannot establish that an event outside the network actually occurred. If every validator receives the same false but properly authorised input, agreement among validators does not turn that input into a true statement.

Finality of an accepted record

Finality describes the point at which a transaction is considered settled or no longer expected to be reversed under the applicable network rules. Some systems provide stronger or faster finality than others. Therefore, the presence of blockchain technology does not imply that every transaction becomes irreversible immediately after submission.

Prelims focus

  • Consensus establishes the accepted ledger state or transaction history.
  • Consensus does not always require unanimous approval by all nodes.
  • Bitcoin uses Proof of Work.
  • Ethereum has used Proof of Stake since September 2022.
  • Permissioned networks restrict validation to authorised participants.
  • Trap: Consensus about a record does not independently prove that the recorded real-world event is true.

[Ethereum.org, Consensus Mechanisms and Proof-of-Stake documentation, consulted 5 November 2026; NIST, Blockchain, validation and consensus rules, consulted 5 November 2026; UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Distributed Ledger Technology section, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Consensus provides a common accepted history when several nodes receive proposed transactions.

title: Consensus: How Participants Agree on a Shared Ledger

body:
Meaning of a smart contract

A conventional agreement describes obligations between people or organisations. A smart contract, in blockchain terminology, is a computer program deployed within a blockchain system that carries out predefined operations when its conditions are satisfied.

A smart contract is program code and associated data that a blockchain network executes according to defined rules, with the resulting changes recorded according to the network's procedures.

The expression smart contract does not mean that the program can understand human intentions or exercise legal judgment. It follows the instructions written into it.

How the rules operate

A simple smart-contract arrangement can be understood through 3 elements:

  • Condition: A specified event or requirement must be satisfied.
  • Action: The program performs the operation associated with that condition.
  • Record: The resulting operation or state change becomes part of the blockchain's accepted records.

For example, a commercial arrangement may provide that payment is released after an authorised warehouse confirms delivery of goods and the required invoice conditions are met. The smart contract can check the recorded conditions and initiate a permitted digital operation. Actual payment also depends on the payment mechanism and any external system connected to the arrangement.

Smart contracts and real-world information

A smart contract can reliably process information available to it, but it cannot independently inspect a real delivery or determine whether medicines are genuine. It must receive relevant information from an authorised person, device or external service.

An external information provider that supplies data to a blockchain application is sometimes called an oracle. The term refers to a source or mechanism providing information, not to a guarantee that the information is correct.

If a warehouse employee falsely confirms delivery, the smart contract may execute its instructions correctly while producing an undesirable result. The reliability of the complete system therefore depends on both the program and the accuracy of its inputs.

Advantages and limitations

Smart contracts may reduce repeated manual checks, apply the same rules consistently and create an auditable record of automated actions. They can be useful for straightforward processes with clearly defined conditions.

However, software mistakes, inadequate permissions, misleading external data and poorly framed conditions can cause problems. A program does not automatically resolve disputes about quality, fraud, legal ownership or contractual interpretation. These matters may still require human decisions and applicable legal procedures.

Smart contract versus legal contract: A smart contract describes executable digital rules. A legally enforceable contract depends on the applicable law and the parties' agreement. The 2 may be connected, but they are not automatically identical.

Can a smart contract be changed?

Once deployed, the code of a smart contract on some blockchains cannot simply be edited in place. Other systems support controlled upgrades or replacement through explicitly designed governance arrangements. Consequently, smart contracts should not be described as universally impossible to update.

For public administration, the authority to change a rule, correct an error or suspend an automated process must be defined in advance. Technical automation does not remove administrative accountability.

Prelims focus

  • A smart contract is executable program code associated with a blockchain.
  • It operates according to predefined conditions and instructions.
  • Smart-contract results are recorded under the network's rules.
  • External information may come from an oracle or authorised participant.
  • Smart contracts do not independently verify physical events or guarantee legal enforceability.
  • Trap: A smart contract is not necessarily a legally enforceable agreement merely because it executes automatically.

[NIST Computer Security Resource Center, Glossary, Smart Contract, consulted 5 November 2026; Ethereum.org, Introduction to Smart Contracts, Automatic Execution and Predictable Outcomes sections, consulted 5 November 2026; NIST, Blockchain Technology Overview, NISTIR 8202, October 2018.]
